cards.title: Mortality of 2×2 integer matrix semigroups
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that, for every finite list A₁,…,A_m of 2×2 integer matrices, halts and correctly decides whether there exist ℓ≥1 and indices i₁,…,i_ℓ∈{1,…,m} with A_i₁ A_i₂ ⋯ A_i_ℓ=0₂?
cards.why: A minimal-dimensional undecidability frontier for matrix products and discrete dynamical systems.

cards.definitions: The input explicitly gives m≥0 and all four entries of each A_i as signed binary integers. Entries have no magnitude or sign restriction, and m is part of the input, not a fixed constant. Products use ordinary exact integer matrix multiplication: (AB)_(r,s)=∑_{t=1}² A_(r,t)B_(t,s). The target 0₂ is the matrix with all four entries zero. The product length ℓ is finite but unbounded, and generator indices may repeat in any order. Only listed generators can be used; inverses are not supplied automatically. The empty product is excluded, and an empty list is a NO instance. The semigroup generated by the list is the set of all such nonempty products, so mortality means membership of 0₂ in that set. The machine must return YES exactly for mortal lists and NO otherwise, terminating on both kinds. No running-time or memory bound is imposed beyond finite termination; there is no oracle, numerical tolerance or real-arithmetic primitive.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer gives a uniform decision algorithm with proofs of correctness and termination on every finite input list. A negative answer proves that the stated decision problem is undecidable. A procedure that only certifies particular zero products, a bounded-length decision algorithm, or a lower bound against polynomial time does not settle the target.

context_blocks.title: Can a sequence erase every vector?
context_blocks.text: A product equal to the zero matrix sends every two-dimensional vector to zero at once. The question is whether some finite sequence of the allowed transformations has this effect. It is stronger than sending one specified vector to zero: a matrix can kill that vector while acting nontrivially on others.

context_blocks.title: Two small examples
context_blocks.text: Let A=[[1,0],[0,0]] and B=[[0,0],[1,0]]. Neither is the zero matrix, but AB=0₂, so the list (A,B) is mortal. Reversing the order gives BA=B, showing that order matters. The list containing only A is not mortal, since every positive power of A equals A. Thus the presence of a singular generator by itself does not answer the question.

context_blocks.title: Hardness and undecidability are different claims
context_blocks.text: Bell, Hirvensalo and Potapov established NP-hardness in 2012; their 2024 paper still identifies unrestricted two-dimensional mortality as an open decidability problem. NP-hardness leaves open the possibility of a terminating algorithm with very large running time. Mortality is already undecidable for general finite lists of three-dimensional integer matrices, placing dimension two at a basic boundary.

context_blocks.title: Restricted matrix classes have stronger results
context_blocks.text: Jaax and Kiefer prove NP-completeness when each determinant is either 0 or +1. This gives a decision procedure for that promise and does not cover arbitrary determinants. The 2024 membership theorem concerns generators in GL₂(ℤ), whose determinants are ±1; their products are invertible and cannot equal zero. Neither theorem decides mortality when unrestricted singular and nonsingular generators are mixed.

context_blocks.title: Relation to other matrix questions
context_blocks.text: General semigroup membership, discussed in TCS-5921, allows a target matrix supplied as input; mortality fixes that target to zero. A solution of general membership would therefore decide mortality. The April 2026 work on complex matrix embeddings studies different algebraic representation questions and supplies no general resolution of the present integer-matrix target.

sentences: A finite list of two-by-two integer matrices generates all nonempty products with arbitrary order and repetition.
The question asks whether a terminating algorithm can decide if any such product is the zero matrix.
Matrix entries and the number of generators are unrestricted.
NP-hardness is known, while decidability results for restricted determinants do not cover the general case.
Resolving the question would locate a basic computability boundary for products of small matrices.

cards.context:
A product equal to the zero matrix sends every two-dimensional vector to zero at once. The question is whether some finite sequence of the allowed transformations has this effect. It is stronger than sending one specified vector to zero: a matrix can kill that vector while acting nontrivially on others.

Let A=[[1,0],[0,0]] and B=[[0,0],[1,0]]. Neither is the zero matrix, but AB=0₂, so the list (A,B) is mortal. Reversing the order gives BA=B, showing that order matters. The list containing only A is not mortal, since every positive power of A equals A. Thus the presence of a singular generator by itself does not answer the question.

Bell, Hirvensalo and Potapov established NP-hardness in 2012; their 2024 paper still identifies unrestricted two-dimensional mortality as an open decidability problem. NP-hardness leaves open the possibility of a terminating algorithm with very large running time. Mortality is already undecidable for general finite lists of three-dimensional integer matrices, placing dimension two at a basic boundary.

Jaax and Kiefer prove NP-completeness when each determinant is either 0 or +1. This gives a decision procedure for that promise and does not cover arbitrary determinants. The 2024 membership theorem concerns generators in GL₂(ℤ), whose determinants are ±1; their products are invertible and cannot equal zero. Neither theorem decides mortality when unrestricted singular and nonsingular generators are mixed.

General semigroup membership, discussed in TCS-5921, allows a target matrix supplied as input; mortality fixes that target to zero. A solution of general membership would therefore decide mortality. The April 2026 work on complex matrix embeddings studies different algebraic representation questions and supplies no general resolution of the present integer-matrix target.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
